standard_prerequisites.name: The identification of functions periodic with respect to k Lambda with Lambda-periodic functions by scaling, and the even/odd decomposition formulas for f in terms of A(weierstrass) and weierstrass' times B
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Used inside the counted proof at lines 627-630 and 631-634, 643-646
standard_prerequisites.use: Reduces to k = 1 and produces the explicit expressions whose pole counts are estimated.

standard_prerequisites.name: Elliptic functions have as many zeroes as poles, counted with multiplicity
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Used inside the counted proof at lines 640-641
standard_prerequisites.use: Turns the pole bound on A(weierstrass) into the degree bound on its numerator.

core_obligations: Reduce to k = 1: membership in M_{k Lambda} is equivalent to membership of f(kz) in M_Lambda, so it suffices to treat the Lambda-periodic case (proof lines 627-629).

Bound the denominator: writing A(weierstrass) = (f(z)+f(-z))/2 shows that A(weierstrass) has at most 2N poles counted with multiplicity, while A(weierstrass) with A = P/Q in lowest terms has at least deg Q poles (the zeroes of Q(weierstrass)), so deg Q <= 2N (proof lines 630-638).
Bound the numerator: applying the same argument to 1/A(weierstrass) and using that an elliptic function has as many zeroes as poles gives deg P <= 2N (proof lines 640-641).
Bound the odd part: from B(weierstrass(z)) = (f(z)-f(-z))/(2 weierstrass'(z)) the same pole and zero counting gives deg R, deg S <= 2N+3 (proof lines 643-647).
proof_roadmap: Reduce by scaling to the Lambda-periodic case and write f in its even/odd decomposition (proof lines 627-630).
Read the claimed degree bounds off the pole counts of the even and odd parts, using the zero-pole equality for the numerators (proof lines 631-647).
difficulty_reason: The lemma bounds the degrees of a decomposition f = A(weierstrass_k) + weierstrass_k' B(weierstrass_k) for a function f in M_{k Lambda} with at most N poles counted with multiplicity: the numerator and denominator of A have degree at most 2N, those of B at most 2N+3 (statement lines 614-624). The proof reduces to the Lambda-periodic case by scaling, writes f through its even and odd parts, and reads the bounds off two pole counts: the even part has at most 2N poles and its reduced denominator contributes as many poles through the zeroes of Q(weierstrass), while the numerator is bounded by applying the same argument to the reciprocal and using that elliptic functions have equally many zeroes and poles; the odd part is handled the same way with the factor weierstrass' (proof lines 626-647). The step that carries the content is the passage from pole counts to degree bounds, which is the classical zero-pole bookkeeping for elliptic functions; the reduction and the odd part are then the same computation. H2.
